# Getting Your Time Back

> "Therefore watch carefully how you walk, not as unwise, but as wise, redeeming the time, because the days are evil."
>
> — Ephesians 5:15–16

Ask a man why he wants to stop and he'll usually give you one of three answers: his conscience, his energy, or his partner.

He almost never mentions the plain slavery of it. Men have bled to end slavery wherever they've found it. Yet here is a man who puts the collar on himself every night and calls it his private business. The strangest part is something he never notices. On the nights when nothing stops him, he does it and wishes he were a man who didn't. The only time the habit looks precious is when he's trying to cut down, or when a week at the in-laws rules it out.

The more of the lies we clear away before you stop, the easier it will be. So in this chapter we'll look at one cost that needs no doctor, no pastor and no argument about whether it's a sin. All it needs is a clock.

## Do the math {-}

Most men call it ten minutes. Is it? Count the scrolling beforehand, looking for something to get you started. Count the half hour afterward when you lie there like a dropped coat. Count the late night and the slow morning that follows it. Call it thirty minutes a day, and you know that's generous. That is a full working day every two weeks. It comes to about a hundred and eighty hours a year, which is roughly a month of working days. Keep it up for forty years and you've spent three and a half working years of your life on it. What did you make in that time? Who did you get to know? The woman in your head doesn't know you exist.

Now and then a man works out what a week costs him, and that's unpleasant enough. He never does the math for a lifetime.

## It was never ten minutes {-}

Be honest about where the time goes. The act is the smallest part of it.

**The hunt.** If porn is still in the picture, you know about the hunt. One coach describes men with hundreds of tabs open, searching for one video they like. If porn is gone, the hunt has only moved. Now it's a scroll through a feed that was supposed to be innocent. Or it's a slow search through your own memory for a scene that still works.

**The chase.** Add the hours lust spends on real women. Count the swiping, the messages you drafted three times, and the evenings spent on someone you knew was wrong for you. Count the money as well: the drinks, the gifts, the subscriptions. None of it was courtship. A man courting a wife is building something. This was the itch, spending your time and your wages on its own account.

**The slump.** You know the half hour afterward, and sometimes the whole flat evening. Do that daily and it adds up to lost days.

**The night and the morning.** The session runs late, the phone runs later, and the next morning is gone before it starts.

**The hours in your head.** These don't show on any clock. They're the minutes at your desk, in the pew and on the train when part of you is already planning tonight.

Then add the biggest cost, which is the things that never happened. The book you didn't write. The business you talked about for five years. The language, the instrument, the friend you never called back. The same coach says the habit leaves you "a man with a bunch of ideas, but zero execution", and every man with a drawer full of half-started projects knows what he means.

## The job offer {-}

Suppose I offered you a job tomorrow. Same work, same pay, same boss, but with one difference: an extra month off every year, fully paid, for the rest of your career.

You'd sign before I'd finished the sentence. Your only problem would be deciding where to go. Yet a man in the trap turns that same offer down every year. Why?

Here's the reason. Every other decision in your life gets weighed. You look at what you'd gain and what it would cost, and you choose. You may choose badly, but you do choose. Whenever a man weighs this habit honestly, the scales crash down on one side, and the verdict comes back in capital letters: "STOP. YOU'RE BEING ROBBED." So he doesn't weigh it. He hasn't decided to carry on. He carries on because he believes he can't stop. And he keeps his eyes off the scales so that he can live with himself.

A young man who fought this for nineteen years said: "I can't tell you how many years I've wasted battling with the lust". Nobody can hand those years back. But he has decades still to come, and so do you.

The men who've stopped all report the same surprise, which is how much room there suddenly is. One says, "I'm actually reading books again for the first time in a decade". Another took up the piano in the space the habit left behind. One man has practical advice for all that room. Pick one goal you could reach in three or four months, and pour the hours into that.

Soon you'll be making your decision, if you haven't made it already. Staying free after that takes one thing: you don't do it, and you don't fall for "just this once". If you're ever tempted by that phrase, remember what it costs. It doesn't cost you ten minutes. It costs you the years.

And if you're ever helping a friend out of this trap, tell him this. You know a man who turned down a month's extra vacation every year with full pay. When he asks who would be that foolish, tell him. It's rude, but it works.

Paul's word for what you're about to do with your time is "redeeming", which means buying back. Moses, who led Israel out of slavery in Egypt, prayed about the same thing long before him, in Psalm 90: "So teach us to count our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom."

You've counted them now.
